ops.old: CMS evaluations of BPCI-Advanced through the first several performance years found that the model generated aggregate net savings to Medicare, with results concentrated in a subset of clinical episodes. Lower extremity joint replacement (LEJR) emerged as the clear savings driver: BPCI-A participants managing LEJR episodes consistently generated savings of 2-5% relative to target prices, primarily through reductions in skilled nursing facility (SNF) utilization. Cardiac episodes — major joint replacement, coronary artery bypass graft, cardiac valve procedures — showed more modest savings, while most medical episodes (pneumonia, COPD, sepsis) generated near-zero or negative net savings.
ops.new: CMS's evaluations of BPCI-Advanced describe a model that saved money only after a slow start. The final evaluation by The Lewin Group, released by CMS in September 2026, estimates more than $800 million in net Medicare savings across the model's eight model years (2018–2025), with spending $700–$1,100 lower per episode — but the first three model years produced net losses, because reconciliation payments to participants exceeded the spending reductions. As in the earlier BPCI and CJR experience, the most reliable savings mechanism was reduced use of institutional post-acute care, which is why lower extremity joint replacement (LEJR), with its historically high skilled nursing facility (SNF) use, became the emblematic bundled episode, while medical episodes such as pneumonia, COPD, and sepsis offered less modifiable spending.
ops.claim: Early BPCI-A evaluations found aggregate net savings; LEJR 2-5% vs target; 'cardiac episodes — major joint replacement'
ops.sources: CMS Innovation Insight 'BPCI Advanced Final Evaluation Shows $800M in Net Savings' (2026-09-23): >$800M net over eight model years, $700-$1,100 per episode; The Lewin Group BPCI Advanced Final Evaluation Report (net losses MY1-3, per phase 6 ledger); Health Affairs 2025 doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2025.00459 (BPCI-A effects on hospital and CMS spending 2018-21)
ops.note: Early years were net losses, not net savings; '2-5%' unsourced; joint replacement listed as a cardiac episode.

ops.old: The CJR evaluation by Finkelstein, Ji, Mahoney, and Skinner, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, found that CJR reduced Medicare spending per episode by approximately $812 (about 3.7%), driven almost entirely by reductions in post-acute care spending — specifically, a decline in SNF use and a shift toward home health. Readmission rates did not increase, and patient-reported outcomes on functional recovery and patient experience were not significantly different between CJR and control markets.
ops.new: A two-year evaluation by Barnett, Wilcock, McWilliams and colleagues, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2019 and covering 280,161 procedures in 803 CJR hospitals, found that CJR reduced Medicare spending per joint-replacement episode by $812 (3.1%), driven by less use of skilled nursing facilities and other institutional post-acute care, with no change in complication rates. A separate first-year analysis by Finkelstein, Ji, Mahoney, and Skinner (JAMA, 2018) found that CJR reduced discharges to institutional post-acute care but did not find a statistically significant change in spending in the program's first year.
ops.sources: Barnett ML, Wilcock A, McWilliams JM, et al. Two-Year Evaluation of Mandatory Bundled Payments for Joint Replacement. N Engl J Med 2019;380:252-62 (Harvard Chan news: $812, 3.1%, 280,161 procedures, 803 hospitals); Finkelstein A, Ji Y, Mahoney N, Skinner J. Mandatory Medicare Bundled Payment Program for Lower Extremity Joint Replacement and Discharge to Institutional Postacute Care. JAMA 2018;320(9):892-900
ops.note: The $812 finding belongs to Barnett et al. NEJM 2019 (3.1%, not 3.7%); Finkelstein et al. was JAMA, first-year, with no significant spending change.

ops.old: Hospitals that already had low SNF use achieved minimal savings in CJR, while those with SNF utilization rates above 35% achieved the largest reductions.
ops.new: Hospitals that already had low SNF use had little room to save, while those with high baseline institutional post-acute use had the most to gain.
ops.claim: CJR hospitals with SNF utilization above 35% achieved the largest reductions
ops.sources: No study located reporting a 35% SNF-use threshold; general pattern consistent with Barnett et al. NEJM 2019 and CMS CJR evaluations
ops.note: Specific threshold dropped; general point kept.

ops.claim: PROMIS/HOOS/KOOS studies found similar or slightly better functional outcomes at 90 days and 1 year under bundles

ops.old: Analyses by Navathe and colleagues found that some BPCI participants showed shifts in case mix toward lower-complexity patients after joining the model, consistent with selective referral patterns.
ops.new: Navathe and colleagues found that hospital participation in BPCI for joint replacement was largely not associated with changes in case mix, although patients who had previously used skilled nursing facilities became slightly less likely to have their surgery at a participating hospital — a modest signal consistent with selection.
ops.claim: Navathe et al. found BPCI participants shifted case mix toward lower-complexity patients
ops.sources: Navathe AS et al., Medicare's bundled payment program and hospital volume/case mix (Health Affairs 2018; MedicalResearch.com interview; Commonwealth Fund summary 'Bundled payment program does not drive hospitals to increase volume')
ops.note: Overstated: the study found case mix largely unchanged, with one small selection signal.

ops.old: SNF stays for hip and knee replacement averaged 10-20 days and cost Medicare $15,000-$25,000 per stay — adding 30-50% to total episode costs for patients who were often clinically capable of recovering at home with outpatient therapy.
ops.new: Institutional post-acute care was one of the largest and most variable components of joint-replacement episode spending, often for patients who were clinically capable of recovering at home with outpatient therapy.
ops.claim: SNF stays after hip/knee replacement averaged 10-20 days, cost $15,000-$25,000, adding 30-50% to episode cost
ops.sources: No primary source located for the stated ranges

ops.old: Studies of CJR and BPCI found that hospitals participating in bundled payment for joint replacement showed reductions in SNF utilization for other orthopedic and non-orthopedic patients as well, suggesting
ops.new: Studies of CJR found that hospitals required to take joint-replacement bundles for traditional Medicare patients also cut institutional post-acute discharges for Medicare Advantage patients having the same procedures — patients the bundle did not cover — by a similar amount (about 3 percentage points), suggesting
ops.claim: CJR/BPCI hospitals reduced SNF use for other orthopedic and non-orthopedic patients
ops.sources: Einav L, Finkelstein A, Ji Y, Mahoney N, 'The Spillover Effects of a Nationwide Medicare Bundled Payment Reform' (J-PAL evaluation summary): -3.4 pp institutional PAC for targeted TM patients, -3.3 pp for non-targeted MA patients; PMC10738117 (CJR spillovers, California)
ops.note: Documented spillover is to MA patients with the same procedure, not to other orthopedic/non-orthopedic patients.
